491.title: Valmiki and Narada
491.hook: Narada tells the whole Ramayana in one chapter, ending and all, before it begins
491.howItsDone: Across India and beyond, the Ramayana is retold every year: recited in homes and temples, sung, and acted in village Ramlila performances in the autumn season, by audiences who already know the story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Narada, and Valmiki's question. Is anyone good all the way through? Narada said: I know one. Rama.
screen: `IS ANYONE GOOD ALL THE WAY THROUGH?`

segments.voice: Episode one of a long series. A character turns to the camera and tells you everything: who leaves home, who gets taken, who wins the war, how it ends. Spoilers, all of them, in the first ten minutes. That's chapter one of the Ramayana. Narada answers Valmiki's question with the entire story, start to finish, in about a hundred verses. And people have kept reading the hundreds of chapters that follow anyway.
screen: `EPISODE ONE TELLS YOU EVERYTHING.` → `A HUNDRED VERSES, START TO FINISH.` → `AND PEOPLE KEEP READING.`

segments.voice: Here's Narada's outline. Rama, the eldest son of King Dasharatha, deeply loved, is about to be made heir. But a queen, Kaikeyi, calls in two promises the king once made her: exile for Rama, the throne for her own son Bharata. Rama goes to the forest without a word of protest, and his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana go with him. The king dies of grief. Bharata refuses the throne and rules only in Rama's name. In the forest, the demon king Ravana carries Sita off. Rama searches, befriends the monkey king Sugriva, and Hanuman leaps the ocean to find her in Lanka. A bridge is built, a war is fought, Ravana falls, and Rama comes home to rule, a time, Narada says, when no one grieved and no one died young. The whole epic, in a single chapter. It's known as the short Ramayana. Why give it all away? Because the Ramayana isn't built for suspense. It's built for return. Grandparents tell it to children who already know it. At Ramlila plays each autumn, the audience knows the ending before the curtain rises. The pleasure is being with these people again: how Rama answers, how Sita holds firm, how Bharata says no to a crown. Narada even ends with a promise: whoever reads this story of Rama is blessed by it. It's a story to keep company with.

segments.voice: Think of a story you know by heart, a family story told at every holiday, a film you've seen ten times. Knowing the ending doesn't spoil it; being there again is the point. Breathe that way too: you know how each breath ends, and you keep it company anyway.

492.howItsDone: Valmiki Jayanti, his birthday, is celebrated on the full moon of the month of Ashvin, especially by the Valmiki community, who honor him as their guru; Narada appears across Hindu scripture and is remembered as a great devotee of Vishnu.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samkshepa, the short Ramayana. The whole story told in chapter one, already knowing its ending.

Valmika is a Sanskrit word for an anthill, the tall mound of earth termites and ants build. Tradition hears the poet's name, Valmiki, as the one from the anthill. Why would anyone be named that? There's a story people tell, a story of a changed life, told across India in many languages. But here's the honest part: Valmiki's own Ramayana doesn't tell it. In his own book he is simply a hermit, living by a river, asking a good question.
screen: `VALMIKA: AN ANTHILL.` → `THE ONE FROM THE ANTHILL.` → `A STORY HIS OWN BOOK DOESN'T TELL.`

segments.voice: Start with Narada. He's a devarshi, a sage of the gods, and he turns up across Hindu storytelling: the Mahabharata, the Puranas, folk plays. He wanders between heaven and earth, carries news, asks the question that sets things moving, and in later tradition he walks with a vina, singing the name of Vishnu. In the Ramayana he arrives, answers Valmiki, and leaves. Now Valmiki. Some later texts and retellings say he began life as a highway robber, often called Ratnakara, who robbed travelers to feed his family. One day he stopped a group of sages, sometimes Narada himself. They asked: will your family share the weight of your wrongdoing? He went home and asked. They said no. Shaken, he asked the sages for help, and was given the name of Rama to repeat. He couldn't even say it properly, so he said mara, mara, which run together becomes Rama, Rama. He sat so long that an anthill rose over him. That story is found in later works, not in Valmiki's Sanskrit text. In his own Ramayana, Valmiki is a muni, a quiet sage, and in the epic's last book he steps into the story: Sita will find shelter in his hermitage. Today the Valmiki community, in North India especially, honors him as its own guru, and his birthday, Valmiki Jayanti, is kept each autumn.

493.title: the crow and the first verse (the origin of poetry)
493.hook: a hunter's arrow, a grieving bird, and the first poem, spoken by accident
493.tomorrow: the crow and the first verse (the origin of poetry)
493.howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors Valmiki as the adikavi, the first poet; students of Sanskrit often learn the ma nishada verse early, as the story of how the shloka meter, and poetry itself, was born.

segments.voice: Yesterday: valmika, the anthill, and the robber story people tell. In his own book, Valmiki is a quiet sage.

Narada has gone. Valmiki walks down to the Tamasa river to bathe, his student Bharadvaja carrying his bark cloth. The water, Valmiki says, is clear, the way a good person's mind is clear. On a branch near the bank, two birds, a pair, are calling to each other, lost in each other. Then, out of nowhere, an arrow. A hunter has shot the male. He falls, bleeding, and the female circles, crying. Valmiki watches. Something rises in his throat, and he speaks.
screen: `DOWN TO THE TAMASA RIVER.` → `TWO BIRDS ON A BRANCH.` → `AN ARROW. A CRY.`

segments.voice: What he says is a curse: ma nishada pratishtham tvam agamah shashvatih samah, yat kraunchamithunad ekam avadhih kamamohitam. Hunter, may you never find rest for endless years, because you killed one of a pair of krauncha birds, lost in love. First, the bird. Our title calls it a crow, but the Sanskrit word is krauncha, and translators usually make it a curlew or a crane: big, long-legged water birds, here a mated pair. Now the surprise. Valmiki stops, troubled. What did I just say? Grief made him curse a man, and that bothers him. But then he notices how it came out. Four quarters, each the same number of syllables, a rhythm you could set to a lute. He'd spoken in perfect measure without trying. And he names it: this was born of shoka, grief, so let it be called shloka, verse. That's the tradition's story of the first poem. Not from ambition, not from a court asking for praise, but from compassion for a bird he didn't know. That's why Valmiki is called the adikavi, the first poet, and his Ramayana the adikavya, the first poem. The shloka meter goes on to carry the Ramayana's own telling, verse after verse. All of it, the tradition says, began on a riverbank, with one man who couldn't look away from someone else's grief.
screen: `A CURSE, SPOKEN IN GRIEF.` · `KRAUNCHA: A CRANE OR CURLEW.` · `SHOKA, GRIEF, BECOMES SHLOKA, VERSE.` · `THE FIRST POET: ADIKAVI.` · then, large: `MĀ NIṢĀDA PRATIṢṬHĀṂ TVAM.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: krauncha, and the hunter's arrow. Valmiki's grief, shoka, poured out as verse, shloka.

Valmiki goes back to his hermitage, but he can't let it go. He bathes, he sits, and the verse keeps playing in his head, along with the guilt of having cursed someone. You know the feeling: a sentence you said today, replaying at night. Then a visitor arrives. Not a wandering sage this time. Brahma himself, the creator, four-faced, the one the whole world comes from. And Valmiki, still lost in the bird's grief, can't stop saying the verse, even in front of him.
screen: `REPLAYING IT AT NIGHT.` → `A VISITOR: BRAHMA.` → `STILL SAYING THE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Brahma smiles and settles it. Don't be troubled, he says. That verse came from me; it was meant to. Now tell the whole story of Rama, as Narada told it to you, in this same meter. What's hidden will be shown to you: what Rama did and said, what Sita did, what happened in private and in public. Not one word you speak in this poem will be false. Then the promise people still quote: as long as mountains stand and rivers flow on the earth, so long will the story of Rama be told. Brahma disappears, and Valmiki's students repeat the verse to each other in wonder. Valmiki sits facing east on a seat of sacred grass, sips water, and turns inward. The story comes to him, the book says, in vision, all of it, laughter, talk, walks, as clearly as if it were in front of him. He composes it. The tradition gives the count: twenty-four thousand verses, in what we now know as seven books. Then he needs someone to carry it. Two boys live in his hermitage, twins with beautiful voices, Kusha and Lava. He teaches them the whole poem by heart, and they sing it at gatherings of sages and later in a king's court. Here's the turn: the twins are Rama's own sons, though Rama doesn't know them yet. The story will be sung to its own hero.

495.title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
495.hook: a city where everyone is content, and the one man in it who isn't
495.howItsDone: Ayodhya, on the Sarayu river in today's Uttar Pradesh, is revered in Hindu tradition as Rama's birthplace and is a place of pilgrimage; the Bala Kanda's opening chapters describe the city and its king.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the crow and the first verse, and Brahma's promise. As long as mountains stand, Rama's story will be told, and two boys learned it by heart.

The first thing Valmiki gives us is a city. Ayodhya, on the river Sarayu, in the land of Kosala. Wide straight roads sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers, gates and arches, music, merchants, horses, elephants, full granaries. In his telling, nobody there is greedy, nobody lies, nobody is without learning or without food. A city working as it should. And at its center sits a king who has everything, and who can't sleep for wanting the one thing he doesn't have.
screen: `AYODHYA, ON THE SARAYU.` → `A CITY WORKING AS IT SHOULD.` → `A KING WHO CAN'T SLEEP.`

segments.voice: The king is Dasharatha, of the line of Ikshvaku. His name means ten chariots, and tradition explains it as one whose chariot could go in all ten directions. He's wise, generous, a famous warrior, guided by great counselors like the sage Vasishtha. He has three chief queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And he has no son. For a king in the epic's world, that isn't only personal sorrow. It's the line, the ancestors' rites, the kingdom's future. So Dasharatha thinks it through and decides: I will perform the ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice, for the sake of sons. Notice how he does it. He doesn't act alone. He calls his priests and ministers, lays out his grief and his plan, and asks. They approve. Then his charioteer and counselor, Sumantra, takes him aside with a story. Long ago, he says, he heard sages foretell this very moment: a king of Ikshvaku's line, longing for sons, would bring a certain young sage to his sacrifice, and sons would come. The sage's name is Rishyashringa, and his story is strange enough to take all of tomorrow. So the Ramayana's first real scene isn't heroic at all. It's a good man with everything, admitting what he lacks to the people around him, and asking for help.

Deep in a forest lives a sage, Vibhandaka, and his son, Rishyashringa. The boy has grown up with only his father, the trees, the sacred fire and the animals. He has never been to a town, never seen anyone but his father. Meanwhile, in the kingdom of Anga, a long way off, the rain has stopped. Fields crack. Wells sink. The king, Romapada, asks his priests what to do, and they give him an odd answer: bring the forest boy here, and the rain will come with him.
screen: `A BOY WHO'S ONLY SEEN HIS FATHER.` → `A KINGDOM WITHOUT RAIN.` → `BRING THE FOREST BOY.`

segments.voice: Here's how Sumantra tells it. The king's people can't just march in and take a sage's son. So they send young women from the city into the forest, with sweets and garlands. Rishyashringa, who has never met anyone, thinks they're young hermits from another ashram, and welcomes them with water and fruit, as a host should. They give him sweets he takes for a new kind of fruit, and invite him to their hermitage. He goes with them, all the way to Anga, and the moment he enters the kingdom, the rain pours down. The king honors him and gives him his daughter, Shanta, in marriage. That's the story Sumantra brings to Dasharatha, who goes himself to Anga, to his old friend Romapada, and brings Rishyashringa and Shanta home to Ayodhya with great honor. Then the sacrifice. On the bank of the Sarayu, the horse is released to wander for a year, followed by guards, and when it returns the great rite is performed: altars of brick, priests from far kingdoms, gifts given away on an enormous scale. Why the rain story? It tells us who Rishyashringa is: so untouched, so simple and so full of tapas that the sky answers wherever he goes. And in this telling, nobody seizes him. He is invited, and he comes.

497.title: Dasharatha's sacrifice
497.hook: a demon king who asked for protection from everyone except people
497.carry: four sons, born to answer a boast
497.howItsDone: Hindus celebrate Rama Navami, Rama's birthday, on the ninth day of the bright half of Chaitra, with fasting, temple worship, readings of the Ramayana, and in some places a cradle for the infant Rama.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's sacrifice, and your line, where he goes, rain follows. Rishyashringa came, and a horse was set free for a year.

While the priests on earth pour offerings into Dasharatha's fire, the gods hold a meeting of their own. They go to Brahma with a complaint. Ravana, king of the rakshasas, is tormenting all the worlds, and nobody can stop him. Why not? Because Brahma himself gave him a boon. Ravana asked never to be killed by gods, or demons, or celestial beings of any kind. He listed nearly everyone, and left out one group, because he thought them too weak to bother with.
screen: `THE GODS HOLD A MEETING.` → `RAVANA'S BOON.` → `HE LEFT OUT ONE GROUP.`

segments.voice: Ravana left out human beings. He scorned them. So Brahma says: he can be killed by a human. And Vishnu arrives, and agrees to be born as a man, in four parts, as the four sons of Dasharatha. Down on earth, Rishyashringa begins a second rite, for the sake of sons. Out of the fire rises a great shining being, carrying a golden vessel with a silver lid. Inside is payasa, sweet rice cooked in milk, made by the gods. Give this to your queens, he tells Dasharatha. The king, overjoyed, divides it. Half to Kausalya. Of the rest, a share to Sumitra, then a share to Kaikeyi, then the last share to Sumitra again. In time, four sons are born. Rama to Kausalya, on the ninth day of the bright half of the month of Chaitra, the day Hindus still celebrate as Rama Navami. Bharata to Kaikeyi. And to Sumitra, with her two shares, twins: Lakshmana and Shatrughna. The loophole is the whole point: a king who torments every world will be undone by the one thing he thought didn't count. Now the week, from the top. Narada's whole story in one chapter. The poet from the anthill. A krauncha bird, and grief becoming verse. Brahma's promise and the singing twins. A king who asked for help. A rain-bringing sage. And today, four boys, born to answer a boast.
screen: `RAVANA SCORNED HUMAN BEINGS.` · `A VESSEL OF PAYASA FROM THE FIRE.` · `FOUR SONS, AND RAMA NAVAMI.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `RAMA, BHARATA, LAKSHMANA, SHATRUGHNA.`
